correctness.rationale: The decomposition is correct and supplies the required infinite proof. Writing an exponential-perfect integer uniquely as \(n=cm\), with \(c\) the product of prime powers having exponent at least two and \(m\) its coprime squarefree part, multiplicativity and \(\sigma^{(e)}(m)=m\) show that \(n\) is exponential-perfect exactly when \(c\) is. Hagis's primary paper uses this same powerful-core decomposition and records the prior finiteness theorem for powerful exponential-perfect numbers with fewer than any prescribed number of prime factors. The later handbook explicitly records the prior classification that \(36\) is the only exponential-perfect integer with two distinct prime factors. For fixed \(r\), summing Landau's fixed-\(k\) squarefree almost-prime asymptotic over the finitely many cores shows that the unique two-prime core \(36\) contributes \(X(\log\log X)^{r-3}/(36(r-3)!\log X)\), while every core with at least three prime factors loses at least one power of \(\log\log X\), or contributes only \(O(1)\) when \(r=3\). A fresh independent enumeration through \(20{,}000\) found \(175\) exponential-perfect integers and exactly \(36\) in the two-prime layer. This finite check is corroborative only.
residual_risks: The original 1978 Hanumanthachari--Subrahmanya Sastri--Srinivasan paper containing the two-prime classification was not obtained as a reliable full text in this run; the classification was checked in the later handbook and independently through the finite replay.
The asymptotic is for fixed \(r\); no uniformity is established when \(r\) grows with \(X\).

originality.rationale: Hagis proves a global positive-density result by summing squarefree multiples of powerful exponential-perfect cores, and explicitly relies on the finiteness of cores with bounded prime support. The two-prime classification \(36\) is also prior. Neither inspected source refines the global count by a fixed value of \(\omega(n)\), identifies the unique \(36\)-core as the dominant contribution in every fixed layer, or states the consecutive-layer ratio. Current Resultary searches returned the assigned theorem as the exact same-object hit and no earlier fixed-\(\omega\) result. The claim therefore survives best-of-knowledge originality as a natural stratified refinement of the prior decomposition rather than a special case of Hagis's global density theorem.
